newsitem.title: FRANCE: French jobless numbers ease in February.
newsitem.headline: French jobless numbers ease in February.

text.p: The number of people out of work in France showed a surprise fall in February, though economists said this was not enough to suggest that unemployment, the black spot in the French economy, had peaked.
Labour ministry figures released on Friday showed the seasonally adjusted number of people out of work fell by 7,500 to 3.09 million. Economists had expected a small rise.

The jobless rate, however, which is calculated differently and based on International Labour Organisation criteria which exclude people who did some part-time work in the month, rose to a record 12.8 percent from 12.7 percent.

Economists, who focus more on the jobless numbers than the unemployment rate, said monthly figures had become very volatile since the method for calculating them was changed last year and argued against reading too much into the February fall.
They still expected unemployment to rise further, although with the rate of increase slowing, the trend is expected to reverse towards the end of the year as growth picks up speed.
"Overall employment figures have been a little bit better over the last three or four months," Societe Generale economist Vincent Chaigneau said.

"But the improvement is not enough to brake the rise in unemployment. We are expecting a continuation in the rise in the unemployment rate to 13.1 percent in the middle of the year, followed by a stabilisation," he added.
The government was quick to look for good news in the data.

"The French economy has begun to create jobs again over the last few months," Prime Minister Alain Juppe told reporters in Bordeaux. "Not enough to make unemployment fall significantly, but it is a positive element," he said.
Unemployment has risen relentlessly since President Jacques Chirac took office in 1995 pledging to make jobs the priority.
Hemmed in by the need to cut public spending in preparation for European monetary union, the conservative government has been unable to throw money at the problem.
And its attempts to create jobs through a myriad of subsidised schemes have had little effect, simply substituting a subsidised job for one which would have been created anyway.
Its latest drive to redirect resources towards jobs for the young also appears to have taken a toll on long-term unemployment, where job incentive schemes have been restricted.
In February, the number of people unemployed for more than a year rose 0.7 percent from the previous month and was up 6.2 percent from the same time last year, at 1.1 million.

The government is counting on an acceleration in growth -- which it sees at at least 2.3 percent this year after 1.3 percent last year -- to produce a turnaround in unemployment in time for parliamentary elections in March 1998.
But worse-than-expected industrial output data for January released on Friday, suggested that the economic recovery still remained very hesitant at the start of this year.
Total industrial output fell 1.2 percent in January from the previous month, while manufacturing output was down 1.0 percent.

"It highlights the recovery will indeed be slow and growth will not pick up for some time," JP Morgan economist David Naude said. "You have to take account of the fact that data has been volatile recently. I don't think it's worrisome for the underlying trend but the pace of recovery will nevertheless be slow in the first half," he said.
